sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: Latin begins as a formal course in Grade 3 (§3E). The outline calls it the highest-leverage subject in the grammar stage: it builds English vocabulary, makes grammar concrete, and disciplines the memory. In K–2 the child met Latin only as songs, prayers and sayings inside Memory Work; now it becomes a course of its own.

For Grades 3–4 the outline lists vocabulary, the first and second declensions, present-tense conjugations, and Latin sayings (§3E). Grade 3 covers the first half of that: the first conjugation and the verb to be, the first declension, the start of the second declension and second conjugation, and about 120 words. Grade 4 (Latin II) completes it.
Like Arithmetic, Latin sits in both cadences (§7). The forms and vocabulary need spacing, so a short drill lives in the daily core. The lessons live in the weekly queue.

The course uses ecclesiastical pronunciation (Church Latin), the Latin of the Church's prayers and hymns, which the child has already heard in K–2 Memory Work. For example, c before e or i sounds like ch (caelum, "CHAY-loom"), and v sounds like v.
Families who prefer classical pronunciation (c always hard, v like w) may use it instead. Pick one and keep to it.

blocks.text: Why this order. Verbs come first because a Latin verb is a whole sentence by itself (amat: "he loves"), so the child can translate real Latin in week 2. The verb sum and nouns follow. Cases are chanted early, because chanting is easy at this age, but they're used one at a time: the subject (nominative) in Term 3, then the direct object (accusative) in Term 4, in step with English grammar.
Latin and English grammar teach the same ideas, so the two courses are timed together:
Latin teaches sum before Grammar teaches linking verbs, and Grammar teaches adjectives before Latin uses them. In each case one course prepares the other. Neither course needs to change.

Every week the child finds English words that come from the week's Latin words: portō (carry) gives porter, portable, transport; aqua gives aquarium, aqueduct. This is where Latin feeds English vocabulary (§3E), and it's the seed of the Latin and Greek roots in Grade 4's Spelling & Vocabulary (§3A).

Daily drill, Day 5 quiz: 10 vocabulary words and the week's chant. 9 of 10 words and the chant written correctly is mastery. Missed words go onto a "Latin tricky words" card that joins Day 2 every week until known.
Chants must be said perfectly, not nearly: a chant with a slip is still being learned.

Term check (week 6 of each term): about 20 written items (vocabulary, chants, forms, three or four short translations), plus the chants said aloud. 16 of 20 is mastery. Below that, the next term opens with a review week.
Vocabulary drill is well suited to auto-grading on the platform (§8).
Year-end: all the year's chants said perfectly; 100 of the year's 120 words known; and a short Latin passage read aloud and translated with help.

Latin was the language of ancient Rome, and for more than a thousand years afterward the language of the Church, of books and of learning. Many English words come from it.

A Latin verb can be a whole sentence. Amō means "I love". The ending -ō means "I". No separate word for "I" is needed.

A declension is a family of nouns that change their endings the same way. Nouns ending in -a, like puella, are the first declension.

Why do Latin nouns change endings? The ending shows what job the noun does in the sentence. This term the child chants all the endings but uses only the first one, the nominative, which names the subject.
Singular and plural: -a is one; -ae is more than one. Stella is a star; stellae are stars.

The Glōria Patrī from memory.
The Glōria Patrī is one of the oldest prayers of the Church, sung and said in Latin for well over a thousand years:
Glōria Patrī, et Fīliō, et Spīrituī Sānctō.
Sīcut erat in prīncipiō, et nunc, et semper,
et in saecula saeculōrum. Āmēn.
In English: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

Find the words the child already knows: glōria (Term 3), fīlius (Term 4), et, nunc, semper. Point out that Patrī, Fīliō, Spīrituī are in the dative case ("to the Father…"), the third case in the chant, now seen in real use.
